<reason>CON built one sustained, coherent line of attack — that "baseline security standards" either recreate app review's core functions or create an unfunded gap — and pressed it relentlessly across every round. The pressure-question exchange exposed a real weak point: PRO's shift from calling the fee "pure rent" to "pay for what you use" was never reconciled with who funds the platform-wide infrastructure (signed identity, kill-switch database, malware scanning) that PRO's own baseline proposal requires. PRO gave concrete, plausible security mechanisms (signed code, hard API blocks, kill switches) and correctly noted CON's own Android evidence shows most users stay in curated stores, but never closed the funding-gap challenge with a clear mechanism, leaving "modest developer fees" vague and unexamined through to the closing. CON's closing explicitly named this silence, giving it the cleaner final frame. PRO's rebuttals were solid and specific but reactive; CON's rebuttals actively reframed the debate (app store as "kitchen, truck, refund desk," not mere inspector) and better exploited PRO's concessions.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.3]-[B4.5], reframing PRO's "pay for what you use" split as failing to fund the actual externalized risk and noting PRO's own baseline standard (A4.1) is platform-wide infrastructure the OS maker must still build without dedicated funding — a point PRO never resolved even in closing.</best_rebuttal>
